question: What authorial title and sweeping philosophical thesis open the Book of Ecclesiastes in Ecclesiastes 1:1-2?
opt1: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity
opt2: The proverbs of Solomon, ruler of the twelve tribes of Israel: Righteousness endureth forever, but sin is a reproach
opt3: The vision of the royal counselor, son of Nathan, judge in Zion: In the multitude of words there wanteth not error
opt4: The prophecies of the king of Jerusalem, heir of the covenant: Wisdom is the principal thing under heaven
correct: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity
explanation: Solomon introduces his treatise as Qoheleth ('the Preacher'), declaring that all earthly endeavors viewed merely 'under the sun' are transient, futile vanity (*hebel*). Ecclesiastes 1:1-2 (KJV) - "The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity."

question: What fundamental existential question challenges the enduring value of human toil in Ecclesiastes 1:3?
opt1: What reward receiveth the righteous man when his years are numbered with the dead?
opt2: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?
opt3: What gain hath a king from conquering foreign nations when his body returneth to dust?
opt4: What advantage hath the wise over the fool in the assemblies of the elders?
correct: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?
explanation: The Preacher poses the foundational question of the entire book, interrogating whether secular human labor yields any permanent, net profit. Ecclesiastes 1:3 (KJV) - "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?"

question: What contrast between mortal human generations and the physical earth is drawn in Ecclesiastes 1:4?
opt1: The kingdoms of men crumble into dust, but the seed of David endureth throughout all generations
opt2: Human empires conquer the four winds, but the granite mountains of Zion never move
opt3: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever
opt4: Man flourisheth like grass in summer, but the sea remaineth bound by the decree of heaven
correct: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever
explanation: Human generations arrive and depart in fleeting succession, while the inanimate earth passively outlasts them all. Ecclesiastes 1:4 (KJV) - "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever."

question: How are the cyclical, repetitive movements of natural phenomena portrayed in Ecclesiastes 1:5-7?
opt1: The stars march in their orbits and sing at dawn, the clouds drop sweet rain, and the earth yieldeth bountiful harvests
opt2: The stormy wind fulfillith the word of God, the deep oceans roar with praise, and the desert blossoms with lilies
opt3: The celestial lights govern the holy festivals, the seasonal rains replenish the wells, and the river Jordan floweth forever
opt4: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north ... All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full
correct: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north ... All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full
explanation: Nature's tireless cycles—the sun rising and setting, winds circling, rivers filling seas without overflowing—illustrate monotonous, unending repetition. Ecclesiastes 1:5-7 (KJV) - "The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."

question: What sensory limitation illustrates the chronic dissatisfaction of the human condition in Ecclesiastes 1:8?
opt1: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing
opt2: The mouth is not satisfied with honey, nor the body clothed with fine linen
opt3: The hands are not filled with silver, nor the feet rested from wandering
opt4: The heart is not comforted by wine, nor the mind peaceful in royal palaces
correct: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing
explanation: Human perceptual senses remain insatiable; no amount of sensory stimulation can permanently quench the inner craving of the soul. Ecclesiastes 1:8 (KJV) - "All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing."

question: What famous dictum dismantles human claims to historical novelty or technological innovation in Ecclesiastes 1:9?
opt1: Every generation inventeth new instruments, but the folly of the heart remaineth unchanged
opt2: The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun
opt3: New kingdoms arise with mighty chariots, yet all fall into the same ancient graves
opt4: Wisdom discovereth deep secrets, but the simple understand not the works of God
correct: The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun
explanation: Under the sun, history endlessly repeats fundamental patterns of existence; true absolute novelty is non-existent. Ecclesiastes 1:9 (KJV) - "The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun."

question: Why do subsequent generations falsely imagine that their experiences are entirely unprecedented in Ecclesiastes 1:11?
opt1: Because the ancient scrolls were burned in the destructions of foreign wars
opt2: Because the elders refuse to transmit ancestral knowledge unto rebellious youth
opt3: There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after
opt4: Because human pride blindeth each generation to the historical chronicles of kings
correct: There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after
explanation: Historical amnesia blinds mankind: previous achievements are forgotten, and future generations will likewise forget current triumphs. Ecclesiastes 1:11 (KJV) - "There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after."

question: What universal existential burden did God assign to the human race to be exercised therewith in Ecclesiastes 1:13?
opt1: A holy warfare against idolatrous nations throughout all their borders
opt2: A perpetual priesthood of sacrifice to atone for ancestral iniquities
opt3: A covenantal pilgrimage of forty years through barren deserts
opt4: This sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith
correct: This sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith
explanation: God has subjected fallen humanity to the agonizing intellectual and physical toil ('sore travail') of seeking to comprehend life under the sun. Ecclesiastes 1:13 (KJV) - "And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith."

question: What immutable limitation of a fallen, broken world is aphoristically stated in Ecclesiastes 1:15?
opt1: That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered
opt2: That which is broken cannot be healed, and that which is dead cannot be awakened
opt3: That which is written in the law cannot be altered, and that which is sworn cannot be annulled
opt4: The depth of the sea cannot be measured, and the flight of the eagle cannot be tracked
correct: That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered
explanation: Fallen human power is fundamentally incapable of rectifying the moral and existential distortions inherent in a cursed cosmos. Ecclesiastes 1:15 (KJV) - "That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered."

question: What sobering, painful paradox accompanies the vast accumulation of human wisdom in Ecclesiastes 1:18?
opt1: For in much wisdom is great wealth: but he that accumulateth silver attracteth thieves
opt2: For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow
opt3: For in much knowledge is royal honor: but he that ruleth a nation suffereth sleeplessness
opt4: For in much learning is spiritual pride: but he that boasteth of understanding shall be humbled
correct: For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow
explanation: Expanded intellectual insight does not produce unmitigated bliss; it sharpens perception of life's tragedies, multiplying inner grief. Ecclesiastes 1:18 (KJV) - "For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow."

question: What psychological and sensual experiments did Solomon undertake to test human happiness in Ecclesiastes 2:1-3?
opt1: I fasted forty days in the wilderness of Judea, and refused to drink water or eat bread
opt2: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure ... I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly
opt3: I gathered ten thousand soldiers from the tribes of Israel, and conquered all the kings of Syria
opt4: I consulted the astrologers of Chaldea, and inquired of the omens of the stars
correct: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure ... I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly
explanation: Solomon systematically tested hedonistic indulgence—laughter, mirth, and wine—while attempting to maintain philosophical detachment. Ecclesiastes 2:1, 3 (KJV) - "I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity ... I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life."

question: What extensive architectural, horticultural, and infrastructural projects did the royal Preacher execute in Ecclesiastes 2:4-6?
opt1: I erected stone altars upon Mount Carmel, carved twelve cedar columns for the sanctuary, and dug silver mines in the hills of Edom
opt2: I fortified the walls of Jerusalem with iron towers, constructed deep moats around Zion, and built granaries in every city
opt3: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees
opt4: I cleared the forests of Lebanon, paved marble highways to the Great Sea, and established trading harbors at Ezion-geber
correct: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees
explanation: Solomon engaged in unparalleled civic works: royal residences, vineyards, botanical gardens, fruit orchards, and sophisticated irrigation reservoirs. Ecclesiastes 2:4-6 (KJV) - "I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards: I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits: I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:"

question: What immense personal retinue, musical entertainment, and royal wealth did Solomon amass in Ecclesiastes 2:7-8?
opt1: A standing army of forty thousand charioteers, tribute from twelve foreign kingdoms, and priests chanting before the ark
opt2: Trained lions from Egypt, fleets of ivory merchant ships from Tarshish, and royal guards of foreign mercenaries
opt3: A company of prophets from Shiloh, scribes transcribing ancient laws, and treasuries filled with lapis lazuli
opt4: Servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle ... I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings ... I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts
correct: Servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle ... I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings ... I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts
explanation: The monarch acquired enormous households, herds, bullion, musical guilds, and every conceivable sensual luxury available to royalty. Ecclesiastes 2:7-8 (KJV) - "I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts."

question: To what extent did Solomon indulge his personal appetites during his pursuit of pleasure in Ecclesiastes 2:10?
opt1: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy
opt2: I indulged my desires only during solemn festivals, observing strict fasting on new moons
opt3: I tasted of pleasure moderately, dividing my wealth equally among the Levites and the poor
opt4: I enjoyed luxuries only after completing forty days of meditation in the sanctuary courts
correct: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy
explanation: Solomon placed zero restrictions on his hedonistic exploration, indulging every visual desire and sensual impulse without reservation. Ecclesiastes 2:10 (KJV) - "And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour."

question: What comprehensive verdict did the Preacher render when objectively evaluating all his vast accomplishments in Ecclesiastes 2:11?
opt1: Then I rejoiced in the glory of David's throne, knowing that my name would be praised throughout all generations
opt2: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun
opt3: Then I saw that wealth was the supreme shield of a kingdom, securing peace for forty years
opt4: Then I perceived that artistic majesty atoned for past sins, bringing divine approval upon Jerusalem
correct: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun
explanation: Upon retrospective audit, Solomon realized that unbridled material accomplishment under the sun yields zero enduring spiritual profit, culminating in futile vexation. Ecclesiastes 2:11 (KJV) - "Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun."

question: While acknowledging that wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness, what leveling reality troubled the Preacher in Ecclesiastes 2:14-15?
opt1: The fool is exempt from royal taxation, while the wise man bears the fiscal burdens of the state
opt2: The fool lives in carefree ignorance, while the wise man is constantly tormented by foreign wars
opt3: One event happeneth to them all. Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise?
opt4: The fool is praised by the simple, while the wise man is hated by the magistrates in the gate
correct: One event happeneth to them all. Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise?
explanation: Physical death is the great universal equalizer; despite wisdom's clear practical advantages, the wise man and the fool share the exact same fatal mortality. Ecclesiastes 2:14-15 (KJV) - "The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all. Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity."

question: Why did the Preacher develop bitter despair regarding all the laborious wealth he had accumulated in Ecclesiastes 2:18-19?
opt1: Because foreign conquerors from Babylon would inevitably burn his palaces and carry the gold into exile
opt2: Because the civil law of Israel required all royal estates to be redistributed among the twelve tribes
opt3: Because the priests of the sanctuary would confiscate his storehouses for ceremonial sacrifices
opt4: Because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour
correct: Because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour
explanation: He agonizingly recognized that a lifetime of strategic toil must be surrendered to an heir whose wisdom or destructive foolishness cannot be controlled or guaranteed. Ecclesiastes 2:18-19 (KJV) - "Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me. And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity."

question: What psychological torment robs the driven, ambitious workaholic of nocturnal rest in Ecclesiastes 2:23?
opt1: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity
opt2: He feareth the dagger of the assassin and the rebellion of his royal bodyguards
opt3: He dreameth of plagues consuming his cattle and locusts devouring his vineyard
opt4: He wearieth his eyes counting the gold shekels stored within his secret vault
correct: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity
explanation: The obsessive pursuit of wealth inflicts chronic daily grief and mental anxiety that invades and destroys restful sleep at night. Ecclesiastes 2:23 (KJV) - "For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity."

question: What positive, godly conclusion emerges regarding the enjoyment of food, drink, and labor in Ecclesiastes 2:24?
opt1: A man should renounce all physical sustenance and fast three score days to attain divine vision
opt2: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God
opt3: A man should labor solely to build monuments in stone that his name may outlive mortality
opt4: A man should hoard every shekel of silver and deny his appetite until his old age
correct: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God
explanation: True joy does not reside in obsessive striving, but in receiving simple daily sustenance and satisfaction in labor as a gracious gift directly from God's hand. Ecclesiastes 2:24 (KJV) - "There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God."

question: What sovereign divine distribution of gifts versus burdensome travail concludes Ecclesiastes 2:26?
opt1: God bestoweth silver upon the righteous and plagues upon the ungodly: yet in the grave all are equal
opt2: God giveth dominion unto the seed of Abraham, but unto foreign kings he giveth servitude under tribute
opt3: For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God
opt4: God rewardeth the wise with forty sons, but the fool dieth childless before his time
correct: For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God
explanation: God grants authentic wisdom, insight, and joy to the righteous, while sinners are consigned to the futile task of accumulating wealth that ultimately transfers to the godly. Ecclesiastes 2:26 (KJV) - "For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit."

question: What universal principle of providential timing and divine seasons opens the poem of Ecclesiastes 3:1?
opt1: The days of man are numbered as seventy years, and his destiny is decided before birth
opt2: In all the works of nature there is chaotic wandering, and human striving cannot alter it
opt3: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven
opt4: God hath ordained the festivals of the new moon, and all nations must keep holy time
correct: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven
explanation: God has sovereignly apportioned distinct, purposeful seasons for every single event and human experience under heaven. Ecclesiastes 3:1 (KJV) - "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:"

question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the antithetical seasons articulated in Ecclesiastes 3:2-3?
opt1: A time to reign, and a time to be exiled; a time to sacrifice bullocks, and a time to burn incense
opt2: A time to conquer cities, and a time to pay tribute; a time to sail ships, and a time to anchor in harbor
opt3: A time to write proverbs, and a time to keep silence; a time to study the law, and a time to judge the gate
opt4: A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up
correct: A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up
explanation: The catalog of fourteen antithetical pairs begins with the bookends of human mortal existence—birth and death—followed by agricultural and structural cycles. Ecclesiastes 3:2-3 (KJV) - "A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;"

question: What emotional and social dichotomies are identified in Ecclesiastes 3:4-5?
opt1: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing
opt2: A time to shout in victory, and a time to weep in defeat; a time to feast with princes, and a time to fast in sackcloth
opt3: A time to sing hymns of Zion, and a time to lament by the rivers of Babylon; a time to marry, and a time to divorce
opt4: A time to buy land, and a time to sell estates; a time to forgive debts, and a time to demand interest
correct: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing
explanation: Human existence encompasses appropriate moments for profound sorrow (mourning/weeping) and celebratory gladness (dancing/laughing), alongside intimacy and distance. Ecclesiastes 3:4-5 (KJV) - "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;"

question: What final pairs conclude the formal seasonal catalog in Ecclesiastes 3:7-8?
opt1: A time to blow the trumpet, and a time to sheath the sword; a time to crown a king, and a time to bury a prince
opt2: A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace
opt3: A time to plow the field, and a time to thresh the grain; a time to drink new wine, and a time to fast forty days
opt4: A time to bless brethren, and a time to curse adversaries; a time to build ramparts, and a time to tear down walls
correct: A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace
explanation: The seasonal poem culminates in verbal restraint vs speech, emotional polarization (love vs hate), and geopolitical reality (war vs peace). Ecclesiastes 3:7-8 (KJV) - "A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace."

question: What profound truth regarding divine aesthetics and the human quest for eternal meaning is revealed in Ecclesiastes 3:11?
opt1: He hath carved the earth with perfect wisdom: and he hath written his commandments upon the stars of heaven
opt2: He hath ordained judgment for all mankind: yet he hath hidden the year of retribution from angels and prophets
opt3: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end
opt4: He hath given dominion unto man over all beasts: but the mystery of the soul he hath reserved for the sanctuary
correct: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end
explanation: God renders all things fitting in their proper time and implants an innate yearning for eternity (*'olam'*, 'the world') in human consciousness, yet keeps His total work unsearchable. Ecclesiastes 3:11 (KJV) - "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end."

question: What permanent, immutable quality characterizes divine acts and decrees according to Ecclesiastes 3:14?
opt1: Whatsoever God planneth is revealed unto the prophets, that all nations may tremble at his word
opt2: Whatsoever God createth is subject to seasonal decay, that man may seek an heavenly country
opt3: Whatsoever God decreeth can be altered through fervent prayer and whole burnt sacrifices
opt4: I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him
correct: I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him
explanation: God's sovereign accomplishments are absolutely complete, eternal, and unalterable, designed intentionally to evoke reverent awe (*fear*) from humanity. Ecclesiastes 3:14 (KJV) - "I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it: and God doeth it, that men should fear before him."

question: What systemic perversion did Solomon observe in the halls of jurisprudence, and what divine reassurance follows in Ecclesiastes 3:16-17?
opt1: I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there; and the place of righteousness, that iniquity was there. I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work
opt2: I saw the bribery of the magistrates in the gate: and I said, The king shall send his soldiers to purge the courts
opt3: I saw the oppression of the widow in the council: and I said, The civil law of Moses is broken without remedy
opt4: I saw the false witness swearing upon the altar: and I said, The priests shall demand thirty silver shekels
correct: I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there; and the place of righteousness, that iniquity was there. I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work
explanation: Even the sacred institutions of human justice are infected by corruption, yet God has appointed an ultimate, comprehensive final judgment for every work. Ecclesiastes 3:16-17 (KJV) - "And moreover I saw under the sun the place of judgment, that wickedness was there; and the place of righteousness, that iniquity was there. I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work."

question: What common biological mortality and origin do humans and animals share according to Ecclesiastes 3:19-20?
opt1: Man was formed from the clay of Eden while beasts sprang from the ocean: yet both sleep in Sheol
opt2: For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath ... All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again
opt3: Man possesses an immortal soul while beasts perish like grass: but both hunger during seasonal famine
opt4: Man rules over the herds by divine covenant: yet the lion and the serpent fear not his authority
correct: For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath ... All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again
explanation: From a purely empirical, physical standpoint under the sun, humans and beasts share physical breath and biological return to dust. Ecclesiastes 3:19-20 (KJV) - "For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity. All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again."

question: What rhetorical question in Ecclesiastes 3:21 addresses the post-mortem destination of the human spirit versus animal breath?
opt1: Who can discern the spirit of the prophet that ascendeth to heaven, and the soul of the wicked that sinketh to hell?
opt2: Who can declare the resurrection of the flesh from the dust of the sepulchre, when no man hath returned?
opt3: Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?
opt4: Who can measure the duration of the soul in Sheol, or track the flight of angels to the throne of God?
correct: Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?
explanation: The Preacher poses an empirical challenge: who can visually verify or comprehend the upward ascent of the human spirit versus the downward demise of animal vitality? Ecclesiastes 3:21 (KJV) - "Who knoweth the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward to the earth?"

question: What practical philosophy of life does Solomon deduce from human inability to foresee the future in Ecclesiastes 3:22?
opt1: A man should abandon all earthly toil and wait upon the mountaintops for divine signs
opt2: A man should build indestructible granite tombs to preserve his memory across centuries
opt3: A man should record all his wealth on clay tablets and seal them before the elders
opt4: Wherefore I perceive that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?
correct: Wherefore I perceive that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?
explanation: Since mortals cannot glimpse what transpires after their demise, the wisest posture is to find legitimate, present fulfillment in one's God-given daily labor. Ecclesiastes 3:22 (KJV) - "Wherefore I perceive that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?"

question: What tragic social reality regarding systemic oppression under the sun grieved the Preacher in Ecclesiastes 4:1?
opt1: Behold the foreign armies marching across the borders, and the cities burned with fire without remedy
opt2: Behold the widows begging bread at the gate, while the judges drank wine in silver cups
opt3: Behold the bondmen laboring in the copper mines, while the taskmasters beat them with iron rods
opt4: Behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter
correct: Behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter
explanation: The devastating absence of comfort for the weeping oppressed—while tyrannical power monopolizes the side of the oppressors—deeply troubled Solomon. Ecclesiastes 4:1 (KJV) - "So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter."

question: In light of relentless earthly oppression, whom did Solomon judge more fortunate than the living in Ecclesiastes 4:2-3?
opt1: Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. Yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun
opt2: I praised the kings who reign upon ivory thrones and conquer foreign empires with chariots
opt3: I praised the hermits who dwell in desert caves and partake not of the sorrows of the city
opt4: I praised the angels who stand before the throne of God and behold not the dust of mortality
correct: Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. Yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun
explanation: So agonizing is unmitigated oppression that the deceased are deemed better off than the living, and the unborn—who have never witnessed evil—are most fortunate of all. Ecclesiastes 4:2-3 (KJV) - "Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive. Yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun."

question: What competitive social envy drives all successful human enterprise according to Ecclesiastes 4:4?
opt1: All travail is motivated by a desire to honor the heritage of ancient fathers
opt2: Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit
opt3: Every right work is performed to earn an eternal crown before the sanctuary
opt4: All labor is undertaken to secure the defense of the city against foreign invasion
correct: Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit
explanation: Under the sun, even exceptional skill and diligent achievement are poisoned at the root by rivalry and mutual envy between neighbors. Ecclesiastes 4:4 (KJV) - "Again, I considered all travail, and every right work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbour. This is also vanity and vexation of spirit."

question: How does the fool self-destructively react to the burden of labor in Ecclesiastes 4:5?
opt1: The fool spendeth his substance upon foreign dancers and sleepeth in the marketplace
opt2: The fool shouteth curses against the king and is cast into the dungeon
opt3: The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh
opt4: The fool fleeth from the plow and beggeth bread among the Philistines
correct: The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh
explanation: Refusing to work, the indolent fool folds his hands in lazy withdrawal, cannibalizing his own physical and financial existence. Ecclesiastes 4:5 (KJV) - "The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh."

question: What wisdom proverb commends modest contentment over stressed, overextended ambition in Ecclesiastes 4:6?
opt1: Better is stale barley bread among brethren, than fattened oxen in the court of a tyrant
opt2: Better is an humble tent in the desert, than a cedar palace surrounded by foreign enemies
opt3: Better is ten talents of silver earned by labor, than royal inheritances gained through war
opt4: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit
correct: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit
explanation: A single handful of resources enjoyed in tranquil peace is vastly superior to double handfuls of wealth accompanied by chronic anxiety and stress. Ecclesiastes 4:6 (KJV) - "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit."

question: What tragic, solitary existence illustrates the absurdity of unbridled avarice in Ecclesiastes 4:8?
opt1: There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?
opt2: A wealthy merchant who had twelve wives and forty sons, yet starved his servants in secret
opt3: A royal prince who conquered ten cities, yet was poisoned by his own cupbearer at a banquet
opt4: An unlearned shepherd who found a pot of gold in the rocks, yet buried it in the earth until he died
correct: There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?
explanation: The childless, brotherless miser works incessantly for endless wealth he cannot enjoy and has no family to bequeath it to, never asking why he starves his soul. Ecclesiastes 4:8 (KJV) - "There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail."

question: What cooperative advantages demonstrate that 'two are better than one' in Ecclesiastes 4:9-10?
opt1: Because two soldiers can conquer twenty enemies: but a solitary warrior is easily ambushed
opt2: Because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up
opt3: Because two merchants can double their silver: but a single trader is ruined by fluctuating prices
opt4: Because two witnesses establish the truth before judges: but an isolated accuser is dismissed
correct: Because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up
explanation: Companionship yields reciprocal productivity and vital mutual support in times of crisis, avoiding the vulnerability of isolation. Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 (KJV) - "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

question: What practical benefits of mutual warmth and collective defense are celebrated in Ecclesiastes 4:11-12?
opt1: Two oxen plow the furrow straight: but a single beast wandereth from the field; and a team of four is invincible
opt2: Two lamps illuminate the dark chamber: but one candle flickers in the draft; and a golden menorah shineth forever
opt3: Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone? And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken
opt4: Two watchmen guard the stone tower: but one watchman sleepeth on his watch; and an army of ten is unassailable
correct: Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone? And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken
explanation: Shared bodily warmth in freezing nocturnal conditions, shared physical defense against attackers, and the unbreakable strength of a braided threefold cord highlight solidarity. Ecclesiastes 4:11-12 (KJV) - "Again, if two lie together, then they have heat: but how can one be warm alone? And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken."

question: What political paradox proves that youth and teachability surpass entrenched royal arrogance in Ecclesiastes 4:13?
opt1: Better is an ancient monarch who hath forty counselors, than an inexperienced prince who trusteth his peers
opt2: Better is a king who conquereth nations with chariots, than a peaceful ruler who lacketh military valor
opt3: Better is an anointed son of David, than an hundred foreign kings who worship pagan idols
opt4: Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished
correct: Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished
explanation: A destitute yet discerning, teachable youth possesses vastly greater intrinsic worth than an obstinate, aged monarch who rejects wise counsel. Ecclesiastes 4:13 (KJV) - "Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished."

question: What inevitable political fickleness overtakes the popularity of newly crowned rulers in Ecclesiastes 4:15-16?
opt1: There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit
opt2: The elders who crown the king with gold shall demand double taxation upon all the grain of the province
opt3: The standing army shall rebel after ten years and cast the monarch into the dungeon of the city
opt4: The foreign ambassadors shall bring sweet words while plotting war along the northern border
correct: There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit
explanation: Even leaders who ascend from prison to immense popularity are soon discarded by subsequent generations, illustrating the fleeting vanity of political acclaim. Ecclesiastes 4:15-16 (KJV) - "I considered all the living which walk under the sun, with the second child that shall stand up in his stead. There is no end of all the people, even of all that have been before them: they also that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and vexation of spirit."

question: What reverent caution governs one's approach and demeanor when entering the house of God in Ecclesiastes 5:1?
opt1: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil
opt2: Take off thy sandals at the holy threshold, and offer two unblemished bullocks before approaching the veil
opt3: Fast forty days before entering the courts, and wear sackcloth while chanting the psalms of David
opt4: Bring seventy talents of silver to the treasury, and anoint the horns of the bronze altar with sweet oil
correct: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil
explanation: Worshippers must approach the sanctuary with cautious reverence and teachable listening, rather than offering mindless, hypocritical ritual sacrifices. Ecclesiastes 5:1 (KJV) - "Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil."

question: What cosmic distance between the Creator and mortal man mandates concise, sober prayer in Ecclesiastes 5:2?
opt1: Recite the ancient prayers of Moses three times daily: for God is eternal, and thou art transient like summer dew
opt2: Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few
opt3: Weep aloud before the mercy seat until the priest blesseth thee: for God is high above, and man is formed from dust
opt4: Offer lengthy petitions with eloquence of speech: for God weigheth the wisdom of the orator in the sanctuary
correct: Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few
explanation: Because God is the transcendent Sovereign in heaven while humans are finite creatures on earth, human prayers must be characterized by brevity and awe. Ecclesiastes 5:2 (KJV) - "Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few."

question: What strict rule regarding sacred vows is established in Ecclesiastes 5:4-5?
opt1: When thou vowest a vow, thou mayest redeem it with twenty silver shekels if thy harvest faileth
opt2: Vows made in seasons of war are binding, but vows made during sickness may be pardoned by the priest
opt3: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay
opt4: It is noble to make great vows before the congregation, even if thy resources permit only half payment
correct: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay
explanation: Vows made to God are inviolable; failing to fulfill a pledge is utter foolishness, making it vastly better never to vow at all. Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 (KJV) - "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay."

question: Why does Ecclesiastes 5:6 forbid claiming before the temple messenger ('angel') that a broken vow was merely an 'error'?
opt1: Because the priest will cast thee out of the holy assembly and seize thy ancestral vineyard
opt2: Because the angels of heaven record all false testimonies and blot out thy name from Israel
opt3: Because claiming ignorance requires an offering of forty unblemished rams at the bronze altar

correct: Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?
explanation: Making rash promises and excusing them as inadvertent mistakes provokes God's righteous anger, inviting divine judgment upon one's labor. Ecclesiastes 5:6 (KJV) - "Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?"

question: What bureaucratic hierarchy watches over judicial corruption and oppression in a province according to Ecclesiastes 5:8?

correct: If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they
explanation: Oppression operates through layers of corrupt bureaucracy, yet God, who is supreme above all earthly authorities, observes and will judge. Ecclesiastes 5:8 (KJV) - "If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they."

question: What psychological law of perpetual dissatisfaction governs the love of money in Ecclesiastes 5:10?
opt1: He that hoardeth silver shall buy cities: but he that spendeth it upon banquets shall be impoverished
opt2: He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity
opt3: He that multiplieth gold shall be honored by kings: yet his sons shall divide it through civil war
opt4: He that tradeth in foreign currencies shall lose his capital: but he that buyeth land shall be established
correct: He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity
explanation: Wealth can never satisfy the human soul's intrinsic cravings; the more money an avaricious person accumulates, the more he insatiably desires. Ecclesiastes 5:10 (KJV) - "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity."

question: What physiological contrast between the laboring man and the wealthy person is highlighted in Ecclesiastes 5:12?

opt3: The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep
opt4: The laborer drinketh water from broken cisterns: but the rich man drinketh wine cooled with snow
correct: The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep
explanation: Honest physical toil rewards the worker with restful, sweet sleep, while the anxieties and surplus of the wealthy induce chronic insomnia. Ecclesiastes 5:12 (KJV) - "The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep."

question: What severe financial calamity and universal mortal exit are described in Ecclesiastes 5:13-15?

opt2: Cattle stricken by sudden pestilence in the pasture ... He shall depart into Sheol bearing only his linen shroud
opt3: Vineyards burned by lightning from heaven ... He shall leave all his silver to an ungrateful bondman
opt4: Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt ... As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand
correct: Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt ... As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand
explanation: Hoarded wealth often destroys its owner through sudden loss, and just as man entered the world utterly naked, so he departs with zero earthly assets. Ecclesiastes 5:13, 15 (KJV) - "There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt ... As he came forth of his mother's womb, naked shall he return to go as he came, and shall take nothing of his labour, which he may carry away in his hand."

question: What divine prerogative enables a person to enjoy his wealth and rejoice in his labor according to Ecclesiastes 5:19?

opt2: The capacity of a man to double his investments through shrewd commerce with foreign merchants

explanation: Possessing wealth is meaningless without the divine empowerment to actually enjoy it; the capacity for joyful contentment is an explicit gift of God. Ecclesiastes 5:19 (KJV) - "Every man also to whom God hath given riches and wealth, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labour; this is the gift of God."

question: Why does the contented believer not brood anxiously over the brevity of his mortal existence in Ecclesiastes 5:20?

correct: For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth him in the joy of his heart
explanation: A person graced with divine joy is so absorbed in present gratefulness that he does not morbidly obsess over the fleeting transit of his years. Ecclesiastes 5:20 (KJV) - "For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth him in the joy of his heart."

question: What tragic 'evil disease' under the sun afflicts the wealthy man in Ecclesiastes 6:1-2?
opt1: A man who built a magnificent palace of cedar, yet was struck with incurable leprosy before he could inhabit it

opt3: A king who conquered ten kingdoms with iron chariots, yet was assassinated by his own brother at a victory feast
opt4: A merchant who accumulated forty talents of gold, yet lost his sight and could not behold his treasures
correct: A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease
explanation: Possessing complete material fortune and honor yet being providentially deprived of the ability to enjoy it—seeing an alien consume it—is an agonizing tragedy. Ecclesiastes 6:1-2 (KJV) - "There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men: A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease."

question: Why is a stillborn child ('untimely birth') judged better off than a centenarian patriarch who never enjoyed goodness in Ecclesiastes 6:3?
opt1: Because an untimely birth is received immediately into the heavenly temple without passing through Sheol
opt2: Because the stillborn child hath never broken the ceremonial statutes of the law of Moses
opt3: If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years ... and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he
opt4: Because an untimely birth inheriteth an heavenly crown without suffering the temptations of youth
correct: If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years ... and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he
explanation: A long life blessed with an hundred offspring and ancient age that lacks experiential joy and proper burial is worse than a stillbirth that never knew pain. Ecclesiastes 6:3 (KJV) - "If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he."

question: What peaceful advantage does the stillborn child possess over the unfulfilled wealthy man in Ecclesiastes 6:4-5?
opt1: He hath never labored under the summer drought, nor paid taxes unto foreign governors
opt2: He hath never tasted the bitterness of bereavement, nor seen his sons fall in battle
opt3: He hath never been deceived by flattering friends, nor experienced the corruption of judges
opt4: Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing: this hath more rest than the other
correct: Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing: this hath more rest than the other
explanation: The stillborn child entered and vanished in quiet obscurity without ever witnessing or experiencing the misery and toil under the sun, enjoying undisturbed rest. Ecclesiastes 6:4-5 (KJV) - "For he cometh in with vanity, and departeth in darkness, and his name shall be covered with darkness. Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known any thing: this hath more rest than the other."

question: What ultimate biological destination levels the person who lives two thousand years without seeing good in Ecclesiastes 6:6?
opt1: Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?
